e-622.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
e-622.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 10, 0\rangle.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle 10,20\rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
e-622.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨10,0⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 10\,\text{d}t,\int 0\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨10t+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v} (1)= \langle 10,20\rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨10(1)+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨10,20⟩ & =⟨10+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =10+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
C_2 = 20.
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨10t,\,20⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-623.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
e-623.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 2e^{2t}, 3e^{3t}\rangle.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle e^2, 2e^3 \rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=2.$
e-623.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2{e}^{2t},3{e}^{3t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 3{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\,{e}^{3t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v}(1) = \langle e^2, 2e^3 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{e}^{2(1)}+{C}_{1},\,{e}^{3(1)}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{2},2{e}^{3}⟩ & =⟨{e}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,{e}^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=0$ and $C_2 = e^3.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{e}^{2t},\,{e}^{3t}+{e}^{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{e}^{2(2)},\,{e}^{3(2)}+{e}^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{4},\,{e}^{6}+{e}^{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-624.knowledge_point: Finding the Points at Which a Particle is Stationary Given the Acceleration Vector
e-624.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 1, 2t \rangle, \quad -\infty <        t <        \infty.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle 2,0 \rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
e-624.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v} (1)= \langle 2,0\rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,{1}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,0⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=1$ and $C_2=-1.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨t+1,\,{t}^{2}-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨t+1,\,{t}^{2}-1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}t+1 & =0\,⇒\,t=-1, \\ {t}^{2}-1=(t+1)(t-1) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t= -1,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨2t,1−2t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨0,0⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨t2,2+t−t2⟩
b
v=⟨3t2−1,2t−t2⟩
c
v=⟨2t2−1,2t−t2⟩
d
v=⟨t2−1,t−t2⟩
e
v=⟨t2−1,2+t−2t2⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives v(t)=⟨t²+C₁,t−t²+C₂⟩. The condition v(1)=⟨0,0⟩ yields C₁=−1 and C₂=0, so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨2t,1-2t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=1$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t,1-2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2t\,\text{d}t,\int (1-2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},t-{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{1}^{2}+{C}_{1},1-{1}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & ={C}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨{t}^{2}-1,t-{t}^{2}⟩.

after.html:
Question 1
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨2t,1−2t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨0,0⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨t2,2+t−t2⟩
b
v=⟨3t2−1,2t−t2⟩
c
v=⟨2t2−1,2t−t2⟩
d
v=⟨t2−1,t−t2⟩
e
v=⟨t2−1,2+t−2t2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨2t,1−2t⟩dt=⟨∫2tdt,∫(1−2t)dt⟩=⟨t2+C1,t−t2+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(1)=⟨0,0⟩. Substituting t=1, we get v(1)=⟨12+C1,1−12+C2⟩⟨0,0⟩=⟨1+C1,C2⟩.

So, we must have 0=1+C1C1=−1,

and 0=C2.

Therefore, the velocity vector is v=⟨t2−1,t−t2⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨2t,1-2t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=1$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t,1-2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2t\,\text{d}t,\int (1-2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},t-{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{1}^{2}+{C}_{1},1-{1}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & ={C}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨{t}^{2}-1,t-{t}^{2}⟩.
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨22,−22⟩ when t=π4, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨−sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩
b
v=⟨sin⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩
c
v=⟨2sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩
d
v=⟨−sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩
e
v=⟨2sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration gives v(t)=⟨sin t+C₁,−cos t+C₂⟩. At t=π/4, the given velocity implies C₁=C₂=0. Thus option b satisfies both the acceleration and initial velocity.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{1},-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩.$ 
Substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1},-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Question 2
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨22,−22⟩ when t=π4, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨−sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩
b
v=⟨sin⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩
c
v=⟨2sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩
d
v=⟨−sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩
e
v=⟨2sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩dt=⟨∫cos⁡tdt,∫sin⁡tdt⟩=⟨sin⁡t+C1,−cos⁡t+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(π4)=⟨22,−22⟩. Substituting t=π4, we get v(π4)=⟨sin⁡(π4)+C1,−cos⁡(π4)+C2⟩⟨22,−22⟩=⟨22+C1,−22+C2⟩.

So, we must have 22=22+C1C1=0,

and −22=−22+C2C2=0.

Therefore, the velocity vector is v=⟨sin⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩.

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution declares v=⟨sin t,−cos t⟩, exactly option b. Independent verification agrees: its derivative is ⟨cos t,sin t⟩ and its value at t=π/4 is ⟨√2/2,−√2/2⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{1},-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩.$ 
Substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1},-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(4) & =⟨\sqrt{4}+4,\,{e}^{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,\,{e}^{4}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=⟨(3/2)(1+2t)^4+C₁,−(1−3t)^3+C₂⟩. Using v(0)=⟨1,6⟩ gives C₁=−1/2 and C₂=7. Thus v(1)=⟨(3/2)·81−1/2,8+7⟩=⟨121,15⟩, option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨12(1+2t)^{3},9(1-3t)^{2}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,6⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=1.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12(1+2t)^{3},9(1-3t)^{2}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12(1+2t)^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 9(1-3t)^{2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2t)^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-(1-3t)^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨1,6⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2(0))^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-(1-3(0))^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,6⟩ & =⟨\frac{3}{2}+{C}_{1},\,-1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}$ and ${C}_{2}=7.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2t)^{4}-\frac{1}{2},\,-(1-3t)^{3}+7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2(1))^{4}-\frac{1}{2},\,-(1-3(1))^{3}+7⟩ \\  & =⟨121,15⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨12(1+2t)3,9(1−3t)2⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨1,6⟩ when t=0, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=1.

a
v(1)=⟨112,10⟩
b
v(1)=⟨121,15⟩
c
v(1)=⟨32,−49⟩
d
v(1)=⟨−66,21⟩
e
v(1)=⟨85,−8⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨12(1+2t)3,9(1−3t)2⟩dt=⟨∫12(1+2t)3dt,∫9(1−3t)2dt⟩=⟨32(1+2t)4+C1,−(1−3t)3+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(0)=⟨1,6⟩. Substituting t=0, we get

v(0)=⟨32(1+2(0))4+C1,−(1−3(0))3+C2⟩⟨1,6⟩=⟨32+C1,−1+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=−12 and C2=7. Therefore, the velocity is given by

v(t)=⟨32(1+2t)4−12,−(1−3t)3+7⟩.

Finally, the velocity at time t=1 is

v(1)=⟨32(1+2(1))4−12,−(1−3(1))3+7⟩=⟨121,15⟩.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution declares v(1)=⟨121,15⟩, exactly option b. Rechecking gives (3/2)·3⁴−1/2=121 and −(−2)³+7=15, confirming the result.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨12(1+2t)^{3},9(1-3t)^{2}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,6⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=1.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12(1+2t)^{3},9(1-3t)^{2}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12(1+2t)^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 9(1-3t)^{2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2t)^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-(1-3t)^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨1,6⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2(0))^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-(1-3(0))^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,6⟩ & =⟨\frac{3}{2}+{C}_{1},\,-1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}$ and ${C}_{2}=7.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2t)^{4}-\frac{1}{2},\,-(1-3t)^{3}+7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(1+2(1))^{4}-\frac{1}{2},\,-(1-3(1))^{3}+7⟩ \\  & =⟨121,15⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨1t3,t⟩,t∈(0,∞). Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨1,−1⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=4.

a
v(4)=⟨2,92⟩
b
v(4)=⟨1,72⟩
c
v(4)=⟨2,132⟩
d
v(4)=⟨4,132⟩
e
v(4)=⟨4,152⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=⟨−2/√t+C₁,t²/2+C₂⟩. Using v(1)=⟨1,−1⟩ yields C₁=3 and C₂=−3/2. Hence v(4)=⟨2,13/2⟩, option c.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},t⟩,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=4.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},t⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,\text{d}t,\int t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}+{C}_{1},\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1}}+{C}_{1},\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨-2+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=3$ and ${C}_{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}+3,\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(4) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{4}}+3,\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{13}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨1t3,t⟩,t∈(0,∞). Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨1,−1⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=4.

a
v(4)=⟨2,92⟩
b
v(4)=⟨1,72⟩
c
v(4)=⟨2,132⟩
d
v(4)=⟨4,132⟩
e
v(4)=⟨4,152⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨1t3,t⟩dt=⟨∫1t3dt,∫tdt⟩=⟨−2t+C1,t22+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(1)=⟨1,−1⟩. Substituting t=1, we get v(1)=⟨−21+C1,122+C2⟩⟨1,−1⟩=⟨−2+C1,12+C2⟩, so we must have C1=3 and C2=−32. Therefore, the velocity is given by v(t)=⟨−2t+3,t22−32⟩.

Finally, the velocity at time t=4 is v(4)=⟨−24+3,422−32⟩=⟨2,132⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},t⟩,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=4.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}},t⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,\text{d}t,\int t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}+{C}_{1},\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1}}+{C}_{1},\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨-2+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=3$ and ${C}_{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}+3,\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(4) & =⟨-\frac{2}{\sqrt{4}}+3,\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{13}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨3{t}^{2},t+\frac{1}{2}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=2.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3{t}^{2},t+\frac{1}{2}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (t+\frac{1}{2})\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{t}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{1}^{3}+{C}_{1},\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{t}^{3},\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{t}{2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{2}^{3},\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+\frac{2}{2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨8,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨3t2,t+12⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨1,−1⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t=2.

a
v(2)=⟨8,1⟩
b
v(2)=⟨4,32⟩
c
v(2)=⟨4,−2⟩
d
v(2)=⟨8,−2⟩
e
v(2)=⟨12,1⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨3t2,t+12⟩dt=⟨∫3t2dt,∫(t+12)dt⟩=⟨t3+C1,t22+t2+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(1)=⟨1,−1⟩. Substituting t=1, we get v(1)=⟨13+C1,122+12+C2⟩⟨1,−1⟩=⟨1+C1,1+C2⟩, so we must have C1=0 and C2=−2. Therefore, the velocity is given by

v(t)=⟨t3,t22+t2−2⟩.

Finally, the velocity at time t=2 is v(2)=⟨23,222+22−2⟩=⟨8,1⟩.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution declares v(2)=⟨8,1⟩, exactly option a. Independent calculation agrees: v(t)=⟨t³,t²/2+t/2−2⟩, so v(2)=⟨8,1⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨3{t}^{2},t+\frac{1}{2}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=2.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3{t}^{2},t+\frac{1}{2}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (t+\frac{1}{2})\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{t}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{1}^{3}+{C}_{1},\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{t}^{3},\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{t}{2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{2}^{3},\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+\frac{2}{2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨8,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨2,\,\frac{2}{{t}^{3}}⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨2,\,\frac{3}{4}⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the time at which the particle is stationary. Do not round the answer.

The particle is stationary when $t=$
{{field-1}}.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2,2{t}^{-3}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{t}^{-3}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+{C}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨2,\,\frac{3}{4}⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨2(2)+{C}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,\,\frac{3}{4}⟩ & =⟨4+{C}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{4}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=-2$ and ${C}_{2}=1.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨2t-2,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2t-2,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2t-2=0 & \,⇒\,t=1, \\ -\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+1=0 & \,⇒\,t=1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution is $t=1.$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(2)=⟨2,34⟩. Substituting t=2, we get v(2)=⟨2(2)+C1,−122+C2⟩⟨2,34⟩=⟨4+C1,−14+C2⟩. So, we must have C1=−2 and C2=1. Therefore, the velocity is given by v(t)=⟨2t−2,−1t2+1⟩.

So, we need 2t−2=0⇒t=1,−1t2+1=0⇒t=1.

The only solution is t=1.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨8(1-2t)^{3},12(1+4t)^{2}⟩,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,-26⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨8(1-2t)^{3},12(1+4t)^{2}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 8(1-2t)^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 12(1+4t)^{2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-(1-2t)^{4}+{C}_{1},\,(1+4t)^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨-1,-26⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨-(1-2(0))^{4}+{C}_{1},\,(1+4(0))^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-26⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-27.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨-(1-2t)^{4},\,(1+4t)^{3}-27⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨-(1-2t)^{4},\,(1+4t)^{3}-27⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}-(1-2t)^{4} & =0\,⇒\,t=\frac{1}{2}, \\ (1+4t)^{3}-27 & =0\,⇒\,t=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=\frac{1}{2},$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨5,3⟩,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-5,-3⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨5,3⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 5\,\text{d}t,\int 3\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨5t+{C}_{1},\,3t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨-5,-3⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨5(2)+{C}_{1},\,3(2)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-5,-3⟩ & =⟨10+{C}_{1},\,6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-15$ and ${C}_{2}=-9.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨5t-15,\,3t-9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨5t-15,\,3t-9⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}5t-15 & =0\,⇒\,t=3, \\ 3t-9 & =0\,⇒\,t=3.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=3,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

Question 15
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨3,12t−2⟩,t>2. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨15,1⟩ when t=11, calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.

a
t=6
b
No stationary points
c
t=8
d
t=4
e
t=10
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨3,12t−2⟩dt=⟨∫3dt,∫12t−2dt⟩=⟨3t+C1,t−2+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(11)=⟨15,1⟩. Substituting t=11, we get

v(11)=⟨3(11)+C1,11−2+C2⟩⟨15,1⟩=⟨33+C1,3+C2⟩, so we must have C1=−18 and C2=−2. Therefore, the velocity is given by v(t)=⟨3t−18,t−2−2⟩.

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero: v(t)=0⟨3t−18,t−2−2⟩=⟨0,0⟩

So we need 3t−18=3(t−6)=0⇒t=6,t−2−2=0⇒t=6.

The only solution that satisfies both equations is t=6, so this is the only value of t when the particle is stationary.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Points at Which a Particle is Stationary Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨3,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t-2}}⟩,\,t>2.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨15,1⟩$ when $t=11,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
content.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t-2}}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t-2}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+{C}_{1},\sqrt{t-2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(11)=⟨15,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=11,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(11) & =⟨3(11)+{C}_{1},\sqrt{11-2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨15,1⟩ & =⟨33+{C}_{1},3+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-18$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨3t-18,\sqrt{t-2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3t-18,\sqrt{t-2}-2⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3t-18=3(t-6) & =0\,⇒\,t=6, \\ \sqrt{t-2}-2 & =0\,⇒\,t=6.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=6,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.
